Since \(21^{2}=441\ge 420\), the move \(m=420\) is legal for every
\(n\) with \(21\le n\le44\).  
Thus every

\[
n_{0}\in[21,44]
\]

is a winning start for \(\mathcal A\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  A two‑move win for the interval \([13,20]\)

The number  

\[
m=168=2^{3}\cdot3\cdot7
\]

has largest prime‑power divisor \(8\); consequently  

\[
\frac{168}{p^{a}}\in\{21,24,28,42\}\ge 21 .
\]

Because \(13^{2}=169\ge168\), the move \(m=168\) is legal for every
\(n\) with \(13\le n\le20\).  
After \(\mathcal B\)’s reply the integer is at least 21, which belongs to the
previous winning interval, so \(\mathcal A\) wins on his next turn.

Hence all

\[
n_{0}\in[13,20]
\]

are winning.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Winning starts below 13

*For \(n_{0}=11,12\).*  
Write  

\[
m=105=3\cdot5\cdot7 .
\]

The largest prime‑power divisor of 105 is \(7\); therefore  

\[
\frac{105}{p^{a}}\in\{15,21,35\}\ge 13 .
\]

Because \(12^{2}=144\ge105\), the move is legal for \(n=11,12\).  
All possible replies of \(\mathcal B\) lead to a number \(\ge13\), a
winning position (the previous paragraph).  Hence 11 and 12 are winning.

*For \(n_{0}=8,9,10\).*  
Write  

\[
m=60=2^{2}\cdot3\cdot5 .
\]

The largest prime‑power divisor of 60 is \(4\); therefore  

\[
\frac{60}{p^{a}}\in\{12,15,20,30\}\ge 12 .
\]

Since \(10^{2}=100\ge60\), the move is legal for \(n=8,9,10\).  
All possible results of \(\mathcal B\) are at least 12, which have just been shown
to be winning, so 8, 9, 10 are winning as well.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Why the numbers \(2,3,4,5,6,7\) are losing for \(\mathcal A\)

For a position \(n\) to be winning for \(\mathcal A\) there must exist a legal
choice \(m\) such that **every** possible reply of \(\mathcal B\) leaves a
winning position for \(\mathcal A\).  
If we denote by  

\[
Q(m)=\max\{p^{a}\;|\;p^{a}\text{ divides }m\}
\]

the largest prime‑power divisor of \(m\), then the smallest number that
\(\mathcal B\) can force is \(m/Q(m)\).  
Consequently a necessary condition for a winning move is  

\[
\frac{m}{Q(m)}\ge 8 .
\tag{1}
\]

When \(n\le7\) we have \(m\le n^{2}\le49\).  A direct inspection of all
composite numbers \(m\) with \(n\le m\le n^{2}\) shows that the
largest possible value of \(m/Q(m)\) is only \(6\) (for \(m=30\)).  
Thus condition (1) can never be satisfied; whatever \(m\) \(\mathcal A\) writes,
\(\mathcal B\) can reply with a number \(\le 7\).  
These numbers have already been proved to be losing, so the whole play can be
kept forever in the set \(\{2,3,4,5,6,7\}\).  Hence \(\mathcal A\) has **no**
strategy that forces the appearance of 1990, and consequently the
starting positions \(2,3,4,5,6,7\) are losing for \(\mathcal A\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

         n_{0}\ge 8,\\[2mm]
\text{A cannot force a win } &\Longleftrightarrow
         n_{0}\in\{2,3,4,5,6,7\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
